title: Research Task Sorter
creator: Dan McCreary
subject: AI for EE Research
description: Sorting activity in which learners place ten everyday electrical engineering research tasks into one of three groups: AI drafts, you verify; You decide, AI assists; or You do directly. Each committed placement gets immediate Correct or Not quite feedback with a one-sentence reason, and each run ends with a score out of 10, a mastery statement at 8 of 10, and the list of missed cards.

educational.topic: Dividing research work between AI tools and the researcher
learningObjectives: Differentiate ten research tasks into "AI drafts, you verify", "You decide, AI assists", and "You do directly", matching the answer key in at least 8 of 10 tasks
Explain why a task belongs in its group using the distinction between cheap verification, judgment that depends on the researcher's knowledge, and responsibility that cannot be delegated
prerequisites: The five everyday research tasks: literature search, data analysis, brainstorming, scientific coding, and manuscript preparation
The definitions of the three groups AI drafts, you verify; You decide, AI assists; and You do directly

accessibility.notes: describe() provides a screen-reader description; all controls are native HTML buttons reachable with the Tab key; correct and incorrect feedback uses words and symbols as well as color; all text is 16 px or larger.

controls.label: AI drafts, you verify
controls.purpose: Commits the current card to the group AI drafts, you verify. Disabled after the placement is committed.

controls.label: You decide, AI assists
controls.purpose: Commits the current card to the group You decide, AI assists. Disabled after the placement is committed.

controls.label: You do directly
controls.purpose: Commits the current card to the group You do directly. Disabled after the placement is committed.

controls.label: Next Card / See Score / Run Again
controls.purpose: Enabled after a placement is committed. Advances to the next card, shows the score after the tenth card, and on the summary screen starts a new run with the cards reshuffled.

controls.label: More Missed Cards
controls.purpose: Shown only on the summary screen when the list of missed cards does not fit on one page; pages through the list.

pedagogical.teachingStrategy: Forced three-way classification with immediate explanatory feedback and a reshuffled second run
keyQuestions: Who should do this task: the model, you assisted, or only you?
Can the result of this task be checked cheaply?
Does the choice depend on knowledge and judgment that only the researcher has?
Does the task carry responsibility, commitment, or certification that cannot be handed off?
commonMisconceptions: AI output that reads fluently can be accepted without checking
Any task that involves a decision is one the model should make
Tasks involving certification or accountability can be delegated if the model is good enough
assessmentOpportunities: First-run score of at least 8 of 10 placements matching the answer key is evidence of mastery
Comparison of the first and second run scores shows whether the sorting criteria transferred to a new card order
Learner explains each missed card using the Why sentence and the three group definitions
